title: UNIT 4: EVOLUTION
notes: ✓ Evolution → gradual change in the genetic composition of a population over successive generations.

title: 4.1.1 DEFINITION OF EVOLUTION
notes:
✓ Evolution → change in the genetic composition of a population over generations.

✓ May involve mutation, meiosis, hybridization and natural selection.

✓ Accumulated changes can cause populations to diverge and may eventually produce new species.

✓ Evolution explains how different forms of life developed and diversified.

title: 4.1.2 THEORIES OF THE ORIGIN OF LIFE
notes:
✓ Origin of life → emergence of heritable and evolvable self-reproduction.

✓ Major theories discussed:

◆ Special creationism
◆ Spontaneous generation
◆ Eternity of life
◆ Cosmozoan theory / Panspermia
◆ Biochemical origin theory

title: SPECIAL CREATIONISM
notes:
✓ Special creationism → belief that different forms of life were created by a supreme being or supernatural force.

◆ Different versions are associated with different religions.
◆ It is based on supernatural explanations rather than scientific testing.

title: SPONTANEOUS GENERATION
notes:
✓ Spontaneous generation → belief that living organisms can arise directly from non-living matter.

◆ Aristotle supported an early form of the idea.

◆ Francesco Redi showed that maggots came from flies rather than meat itself.

◆ Lazzaro Spallanzani showed that sterilized, sealed broth remained free of microorganisms.

◆ Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment finally disproved spontaneous generation.

✓ Principle → life comes from pre-existing life.

title: ETERNITY OF LIFE THEORY
notes:
✓ Eternity of life → life has always existed and has no beginning or end.

◆ Life is considered an inherent property of the Universe.
◆ Therefore, no original creation event is required.

title: COSMOZOAN THEORY / PANSPERMIA
notes:
✓ Cosmozoan theory → life or the organic material needed for life came to Earth from elsewhere in the Universe.

◆ Proposed by Richter (1865).
◆ Suggested resistant spores or germs may have arrived with cosmic dust or meteorites.
◆ Helmholz (1884) also suggested that protoplasm could have reached Earth through meteorites.

✓ Main idea → life originated elsewhere and reached Earth.

title: BIOCHEMICAL ORIGIN THEORY
notes:
✓ Biochemical origin / abiogenesis → life originated through a series of biochemical reactions that produced organic molecules, which became organized into pre-cells and eventually cells.

◆ Oparin → proposed the idea in 1924.

◆ Haldane → independently proposed similar ideas in 1929.

◆ Simple substances in the early atmosphere formed increasingly complex organic molecules.

◆ Miller's spark-discharge experiment produced organic compounds from simple substances under simulated early-Earth conditions.

✓ Key idea → simple chemicals → organic molecules → pre-cells → cells.

title: FIRST ORGANISMS & EARLY LIFE
notes:
✓ The first organisms appeared about 4 billion years ago.

1 They were prokaryotic and lacked a true nucleus.
2 Early organisms likely used RNA as genetic material.
3 Cyanobacteria were among the earliest photoautotrophs and contributed greatly to increasing free oxygen in the atmosphere.

title: 4.1.2 THEORIES OF EVOLUTION
notes:
✓ Major evolutionary theories discussed:

◆ Lamarckism → inheritance of acquired characteristics.
◆ Darwinism → evolution by natural selection.
◆ Neo-Darwinism → Darwin's natural selection combined with modern knowledge of genetics.

title: LAMARCKISM
notes:
✓ Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed the inheritance of acquired characteristics in 1809.

✓ Main ideas:

◆ New environmental conditions create new needs.
◆ Use and disuse → frequently used organs become developed; unused organs become reduced.
◆ Acquired characteristics were believed to be inherited.
◆ Accumulation of acquired characteristics over generations could produce new species.

✓ Key phrase → use & disuse + inheritance of acquired characteristics.

title: DARWINISM / NATURAL SELECTION THEORY
notes:
✓ Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace proposed natural selection as the mechanism of evolution.

✓ Darwin's major postulates:

◆ Geometric increase → organisms produce more offspring than can survive.
◆ Struggle for existence → limited resources create competition.
◆ Variation → individuals differ from one another.
◆ Natural selection → individuals with advantageous heritable traits survive and reproduce more successfully.
◆ Origin of species → useful variations accumulate over generations, producing new adaptations and eventually new species.

title: NEO-DARWINISM
notes:
✓ Neo-Darwinism → modern form of Darwin's theory that incorporates genetics, biochemistry and behavior.

✓ Main postulates:

◆ Genetic variability
◆ Natural selection
◆ Reproductive isolation

✓ Associated contributors mentioned → Huxley and R. A. Fisher.

title: 4.1.3 EVIDENCE FOR EVOLUTION
notes:
✓ Major evidence supporting evolution:

◆ Comparative anatomy
◆ Comparative embryology
◆ Palaeontology / fossil record
◆ Comparative biochemistry

✓ Together, these lines of evidence support common ancestry and evolutionary relationships.

title: COMPARATIVE ANATOMY
notes:
✓ Comparative anatomy → comparison of structural similarities and differences among organisms.

✓ Homologous structures → similar basic anatomy and common evolutionary origin but different functions.
◆ Example → forelimbs of humans, cats, whales and bats.

✓ Analogous structures → similar function but different anatomy and evolutionary origin.
◆ Example → wings of birds and insects.

✓ Homologous → common origin → divergent evolution.

✓ Analogous → different origin → convergent evolution.

title: COMPARATIVE EMBRYOLOGY
notes:
✓ Comparative embryology → comparison of embryonic development among organisms.

◆ Vertebrate embryos show similarities during early development.
◆ Early vertebrate embryos may possess structures such as gill slits and tails.

✓ Similar embryonic development → evidence of common ancestry.

title: PALAEONTOLOGY & FOSSIL RECORD
notes:
✓ Palaeontology → study of fossils.

✓ Fossils may include:

◆ Bones, teeth, hair and skin impressions.
◆ Shells and preserved organisms.
◆ Trace fossils → footprints, burrows and coprolites.

✓ Fossils show similarities and differences between past and present organisms and provide evidence for evolutionary change.

title: FOSSIL DATING
notes:
✓ Stratigraphy → determines relative age by studying the sequence and thickness of rock layers.

✓ Carbon-14 dating → measures radioactive carbon relative to normal carbon; suitable for fossils up to about 60,000 years old.

✓ Dating helps establish the sequence and approximate age of evolutionary events.

title: COMPARATIVE BIOCHEMISTRY
notes:
✓ Comparative biochemistry → comparison of molecules shared by different organisms.

◆ DNA
◆ Cytochrome c
◆ Hemoglobin

✓ The greater the molecular similarity, the more closely related organisms are generally considered to be.

title: 4.1.4 NATURAL SELECTION
notes:
✓ Natural selection → process in which organisms with advantageous heritable characteristics survive and reproduce more successfully.

◆ Advantageous alleles increase in frequency over generations.
◆ Less advantageous characteristics become less common.

✓ Natural selection is described in the textbook as the driving force behind evolution.

title: TYPES OF NATURAL SELECTION
notes:
✓ Directional selection → one extreme phenotype is favored; population shifts toward that extreme.

✓ Stabilizing selection → intermediate phenotype is favored; extremes are selected against.

✓ Disruptive selection → both extreme phenotypes are favored while the intermediate is selected against.

✓ All three change the distribution of phenotypes within a population.

title: SPECIATION
notes:
✓ Speciation → formation of new species.

✓ A species → group of similar organisms with similar biochemistry, physiology and evolutionary history that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

✓ Reproductive isolation prevents populations from interbreeding and allows genetic differences to accumulate.

title: ALLOPATRIC & SYMPATRIC SPECIATION
notes:
✓ Allopatric speciation → populations become geographically isolated and evolve separately.

✓ Different environments and mutations cause genetic differences to accumulate.

✓ Sympatric speciation → a new species develops without geographic separation from the original population.

✓ Both can eventually produce reproductive isolation.

title: POLYPLOIDY
notes:
✓ Polyploidy → condition in which an organism has more than two sets of homologous chromosomes.

◆ Important in plant evolution.
◆ Chromosome doubling can allow infertile hybrids to become fertile because homologous chromosomes can pair during meiosis.

✓ Polyploidy can contribute to speciation, especially in plants.

title: DIVERGENT, CONVERGENT & PARALLEL EVOLUTION
notes:
✓ Divergent evolution → related organisms become increasingly different as they adapt to different environments.
◆ Example → humans and apes from a common ancestor.

✓ Convergent evolution → organisms with different ancestry develop similar traits because of similar environmental pressures.
◆ Example → similarities between fish and whales.

✓ Parallel evolution → organisms evolve independently while maintaining a similar level of similarity.

title: HUMAN EVOLUTION
notes:
✓ Humans did not evolve from modern monkeys or modern chimpanzees.

✓ Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor.

✓ Two important human characteristics:

◆ Large brain
◆ Bipedalism → walking upright on two legs.

✓ Human evolutionary history is represented as a branching tree in which ancestral populations give rise to different evolutionary lines.

title: LUCY — AUSTRALOPITHECUS AFARENSIS
notes:
✓ Dinkinesh (Lucy) → important Ethiopian fossil in understanding human evolution.

◆ Discovered by Donald Johanson and Tom Gray in 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia.
◆ About 3.2 million years old.
◆ Australopithecus afarensis.
◆ About 40% of the skeleton was recovered.
◆ Pelvis, femur and tibia show bipedal walking.
◆ Evidence also indicates some arboreal adaptation.

✓ Lucy helped show that bipedalism appeared before large brain size.

title: ARDI — ARDIPITHECUS RAMIDUS
notes:
✓ Ardi → Ardipithecus ramidus.

◆ About 4.4 million years old.
◆ Discovered in the Afar region of Ethiopia; research findings were published in 2009.
◆ Shows adaptations for both bipedal walking and tree-dwelling.
◆ Important for understanding the common ancestry of humans and chimpanzees.

✓ Ardi indicates that the human-chimpanzee common ancestor was not simply chimpanzee-like.

title: BRAIN SIZE & HUMAN EVOLUTION
notes:
✓ During human evolution, brain size and cranial capacity increased.

✓ Australopithecus brain → about 0.7–1.0% of body mass.

✓ Modern human brain → about 1.8–2.3% of body mass.

✓ Larger brains supported planning, tool use, coordinated movement and other complex abilities.

✓ Human evolution involved changes in both brain size and body structure.

title: MODERN HUMAN EVOLUTION
notes:
✓ Homo sapiens first appeared in Africa.
◆ Modern humans later migrated to other parts of the world.
◆ Different environments created different selection pressures.
◆ Traits that helped people survive in particular environments were favored.

✓ Human populations remain one species because extensive gene flow and interbreeding prevent long-term reproductive isolation.

title: 4.1.6 MUTATION
notes:
✓ Mutation → random or spontaneous change in genetic material.

◆ Mutations can involve a single DNA base or larger chromosome regions.
◆ Mutations introduce genetic variation into populations.
◆ Their effects may be beneficial, harmful or have little/no observable effect.

title: POINT MUTATIONS
notes:
✓ Point mutation → change involving a single DNA base.

✓ Main types:

◆ Substitution → one base is replaced by another.
◆ Addition → an extra base is inserted.
◆ Deletion → a base is removed.

✓ Addition and deletion can cause frameshift mutations when they alter the reading frame.

title: SICKLE-CELL MUTATION
notes:
✓ A substitution mutation in the gene coding for hemoglobin can change the DNA triplet from GAG to GTG.

◆ Glutamate is replaced by valine.
◆ The altered hemoglobin produces sickle-cell anaemia.

✓ One base change can therefore affect the structure and function of a protein.

title: FRAMESHIFT MUTATIONS
notes:
✓ Frameshift mutation → insertion or deletion of bases that changes the reading frame of the genetic message.

◆ Changes the sequence of codons after the mutation.
◆ May produce a very different mRNA.
◆ Can result in a non-functional protein or no protein.

title: CHROMOSOMAL MUTATIONS
notes:
✓ Chromosomal mutation → change in chromosome structure or arrangement.

✓ Types:

◆ Duplication
◆ Deletion
◆ Inversion
◆ Translocation

◆ Often associated with chromosome changes during meiosis.
◆ Large chromosomal changes can severely affect cells or organisms.

title: 4.1.7 GENETIC DRIFT
notes:
✓ Genetic drift → change in allele frequencies caused by chance rather than natural selection.

◆ Strongest in small populations.
◆ Alleles may randomly increase, decrease or become completely lost.
◆ Can reduce genetic variation.

✓ Genetic drift = evolution by random changes in allele frequencies.

title: BOTTLENECK EFFECT
notes:
✓ Bottleneck effect → genetic drift caused by a severe reduction in population size.

◆ Natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods and fires may kill most individuals.
◆ Survivors represent only a random sample of the original gene pool.
◆ Some alleles may be lost completely.

✓ Result → reduced genetic diversity and strong genetic drift.

title: FOUNDER EFFECT
notes:
✓ Founder effect → genetic drift that occurs when a small group leaves a larger population and establishes a new colony.

◆ Founders may not contain all alleles of the original population.
◆ Allele frequencies in the new population can differ greatly from the original.

✓ Founder effect = colonization + small founding population + genetic drift.

title: 4.1.8 GENE FLOW
notes:
✓ Gene flow / migration → movement of individuals or genetic material from one population to another.

◆ Immigration → individuals enter a population and introduce their alleles.
◆ Emigration → individuals leave a population and take their alleles with them.
◆ Gene flow can introduce genetic variation and change allele frequencies.

✓ Example → pollen moving between plant populations or people moving between regions.

title: GENE FLOW & SPECIATION
notes:
✓ High gene flow tends to make populations genetically more similar.

✓ Reduced gene flow allows populations to accumulate genetic differences.

✓ Long-term isolation can contribute to reproductive isolation and speciation.

✓ Gene flow is therefore important in determining how populations evolve.

title: 4.1.9 CAUSES OF SPECIES EXTINCTION
notes:
✓ Extinction → permanent disappearance of a species.

✓ Major causes discussed:

◆ Human activities
◆ Climate change
◆ Increased greenhouse gases
◆ Habitat destruction/loss
◆ Natural disasters

✓ Both human impacts and natural disasters can directly or indirectly cause extinction.
